trickyParts: The harness is on the issue volume at /legion/harness and is meant to be inherited rather than rebuilt: setup.sh is idempotent (PostgreSQL 17.11 with pgvector unpacked from Debian packages without root, nats-server 2.10.22, the cluster initdb'd as UTF8 with an ICU en-US collation because this image's default is SQL_ASCII with C collation and two existing tests read the difference), env.sh is sourced and never re-derived, e2e.sh runs Dispatch's browser suite on a lane of the role's own. Every cache (GOCACHE, GOMODCACHE, GOTMPDIR, TMPDIR, PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH) is on /legion: a Go cache under $HOME evicts the pod. The api suite takes about 1000 s and the docs suite about 780 s, past go test's ten-minute package default, so both need -timeout 1800s or a bare run panics at 600 s and reads as a failure.

This pod has no Docker, so internal/dispatch/delivery's own tests (and four outbox rows) cannot run here: they start NATS containers. They are CI's, and the multiprocess test exercises the same delivery code against the real local nats-server.

The riskiest part of the change is the document cursor: a missed advance leaves a room permanently behind the head, refused, failed, reloaded and refused again. Every advance goes through one funnel, and two sites the plan did not name turned out to matter - a committed write's versions must enter the room's cursor while the commit still holds the document's advisory lock (a browser append queued on that lock takes it the instant the commit drops it), and a room must record the head its load read plus every version this process appended during the load, because ygo reports a loading room as absent.

A cold write (one whose fork came from the store, with no room) is deliberately outside the gate: its update commutes with whatever landed since its read, and gating it broke TestABrowserOpeningADocumentMidColdWriteKeepsBothEdits, a case the code already handled.

Round 4 edits migration 0115 in place - duty_passes holds a bucket bigint where it held a began_at timestamptz - rather than adding 0116. Had any environment run it, the same change would have had to be an additive 0116 instead, which is a different patch.

Round 4's mechanism, chosen by the architect from three shapes and recorded with the reasons the other two were refused. A period is now a bucket of the database's clock, floor(epoch/period), recorded and compared as a number; the gate asks only whether a row holds the current bucket. Judging the period from the tick instant was refused because the tick is the process's clock and now() is the database's, which reintroduces exactly the skew the database clock was chosen to remove and whose bound cannot be measured from inside a pod. A tolerance constant was refused because it has to exceed every lease-acquire delay under unknown production load and stay well under a period, which is a number nobody can honestly write down. The bucket needs no constant and does not depend on when the tick fired. Its cost is that period boundaries are fixed rather than sliding, so a pass can run at the end of one bucket and another at the start of the next - never two in a bucket; accepted for these loops because the lease exists against N processes making N times one result's work, a pair across a boundary is a burst of two rather than a sustained doubling, and the webhook sweep's deliveries are claimed individually by its NATS key-value compare-and-set either way.

Round 3 changed three existing lease tests because the behaviour they pinned changed, not because they failed: TestTwoSweepRunnersRunThePassOnceAndSkipOnce (api), TestTwoReconciliationRunnersRunTheTickOnceAndSkipOnce (docs) and TestARunningSweepWhoseLeaseIsHeldElsewhereListsNothing (redeliver) each stopped a runner while its pass was still blocked on a table lock and then read a 'leased pass ran' line, which a pass cut short no longer writes. The first two now count getting into the pass - ran or cut short - which is the property each row is about and which the shutdown change does not touch; the third's stand-in holder takes its lease on a context of its own, since it stands for another process rather than for one shutting down. Nothing was loosened: each row still refuses two passes, and the one that counts GitHub calls still refuses any.

It now adds one, duty_passes (migration 0115), because the architect decided the property stays once per period and the mechanism changes: a lease that is taken and given back excludes concurrent passes alone, and two processes' tickers are out of phase, so each ran the whole pass. The record is what makes a pass another process already made count, and the elapsed-time comparison is made in the database because two processes' wall clocks differ. Leadership was the alternative and was not taken: it brings a hand-over to design and drive, where this costs one period when a holder dies.

discoveredComplexity: Round 4's first blocking finding is round 2's defect reached through a different door, and that is the pattern worth keeping rather than the line of code. The fix for 'nothing re-examines a room' introduced a queue, and a queue that takes work out before it is done drops it on every path that does not finish - here three error paths, each of which put the room back exactly where the original defect had it. The general form: when a fix turns a dropped event into deferred work, the thing to check is not that the work is remembered but that it is only forgotten by a decision. Three comments asserted the invariant unconditionally while the code held it only on the happy path, which is how it survived a round of review and a tester's pass.

The evidence lesson of round 4 is sharper than its code. Of the two committed two-process rows meant to lock the wake, one passed with the wake unwired - its budget admitted the durable gate's own rescue, a path its own comment named and measured at 6.018 s - and the other never asserted the precondition it rests on, so a slow step would have made it measure an immediate eviction instead. Both were written by a role that had just caught the same shape in its own earlier draft. A row is a lock only against the mechanism it names: the two questions to ask of any regression row are what it does with the mechanism removed, and what it asserts about the conditions its construction needs. Here the answers are now in the rows themselves - a bound between two measured numbers, an attribution to the evictor's own second eviction, and a measured gap that fails the run rather than silently testing something else.

The census's third correction closes this issue's longest-running mistake, and the instrument is the lesson. The first draft read the error mapping in api/server.go and claimed six API route families could answer 503; the second read grep withRoomCursor( and claimed no API write could; the truth is that appendingCursor has two sources and that grep sees one. A contract table is only as good as the enumeration behind it, and the enumeration has to be the call graph of the thing being enumerated - here refuseRoomBehindHead's call sites, then both branches of the cursor each passes it, then each branch's callers. A grep for one constructor is not an enumeration of a function's inputs, and a corrected command without that sentence would leave the next table as likely to be wrong as this one.

Round 2's blocking finding is the cost of a rate limit that drops what it refuses rather than deferring it. The eviction interval was written as 'at most one eviction per room per interval', which is right, and implemented as 'a notification inside the window is discarded', which is not the same thing: the last notification of a burst is always inside somebody's window, and a document nobody writes again notifies nobody again. The shape to look for elsewhere is a throttle whose refusal is terminal - the work it refuses has to be remembered, or the throttle is a dropped message with a timer's name. Here the fix is that the refusal records when the window ends and the room is re-examined then, which is inside the rule rather than around it.

The fix needed a wake on a goroutine that was blocked in a database call, and the honest way to get one was a seam in the shared listener rather than a goroutine of its own. time.AfterFunc's contract is a goroutine per callback, which would have put the evictor's decision beside a notification being decided - the one concurrency shape that component exists not to have - and the cheap alternative, setting ListenIdle to the eviction interval, would have bought the wake with a Postgres round trip every two seconds and an invisible coupling between a ping cadence and an unrelated constant. The seam (NextWake/OnWake, the wait's own deadline) is two nil-safe fields, and its inertness for the other two callers is a measurement in the proof array rather than an assertion.

A pull request GitHub calls mergeable can still be unmergeable in substance, and this branch met both shapes of it in one merge. main deleted two constants this branch's new code names, which no line-level conflict shows and which only the merged tree's compiler sees; and main added a live row that this branch's new lease breaks, which not even the compiler sees. The branch's own CI had been green on its own head throughout. The lesson for a long-lived branch is that the head CI judges is the merge, and that a branch whose base moved under it should be merged and re-driven rather than trusted because no line collided.

The lease defect the merge surfaced is the standby mechanism's own shape turned against it: one lease over two unrelated durables. A lease is a name, and the name decides the blast radius - delivery-consumers covered both durables, so a reconciliation that could never succeed (a denied create, which blocks the client's whole 10 s JetStream MaxWait with the lease held, retried every 2 s because a failed pass is deliberately not throttled) starved the other durable's intake for as long as the misconfiguration lasted. A lease name should be exactly the thing two processes must not do at once, which here is one durable's configuration, not the package's.

Review round 1's blocking finding is the fourth time on this issue that a mechanism was right for the case it was designed against and wrong for a case nobody drove. The live stream's id comparison is sound for a log whose ids only grow; a reset reuses ids, which is the one case the relay beside it exists to handle, and the comparison then silenced the reader for good with the connection open and heartbeating. What let it through is that the reset test calls relay.subscribe directly: it exercises the relay across a reset and never the handler, so the half that fails is the half no surface reached. The rule this issue keeps rediscovering is that a property is pinned only at the surface a user meets, and the regression test for this one is an HTTP request with a since above the head.

Two of the seven review threads were answered by driving the reviewer's own proposal rather than by reasoning about it, and they came out opposite ways: the clamp was confirmed (control reverted, the stream shows nothing but heartbeats) and the cursor routing was refuted (applied at the backfill site, it credits a room with a version it does not hold, which is the fork the gate exists to stop). Neither answer was available by reading. A review finding is a hypothesis with evidence attached, and the cheapest way to settle one is usually to make the change the reviewer asked for and run the test that would catch it being wrong.

Round 5's defect and the proposed fix for it are the same lesson twice: a quantity that carries no record of the scale that produced it cannot be compared across scales. The bucket number 896333757 (two-second scale) against 5975558 (five-minute scale) is the obvious form, and it stopped the reference-excerpt loop for good - durably, so a restart stopped too. The boundary timestamp that replaced it is the subtle form: it is a real instant and so looks comparable, but a two-second boundary is within two seconds of now while the same tick's five-minute boundary is on average 150 seconds behind it, so the comparison skips for all but the first two seconds of each bucket. That one was measured rather than reasoned - five runs out of five red on the tester's row - and it is why the stored period sits beside the stored boundary and the gate counts a record only against a tick of the same period. A later reader will find period_ns redundant with the boundary; the migration's comment says in full why it is not, which is the only defence a column of this kind has.

Three rows now bound this gate from three sides, and no row pins two properties: a lone process must lose no tick (TestALoneRunnerMakesAPassOnEveryTick), a second process inside a served period must make none (TestALeasedLoopRunsOnceAcrossAStaggeredStart), and a loop whose period changes must not be locked out (TestExclusiveDoesNotLockOutALoopWhosePeriodGrows). Each of the three mechanisms tried in rounds 2 to 5 satisfied two of them and failed the third, which is why they are separate rows: a mechanism that passes all three is the thing being asked for, and any one of them folded into another would have hidden the failure that found it.

Round 4's defect is the shape of this whole issue in one line: a mechanism correct for the case it was designed against - two processes out of phase - and wrong for the case the deployment actually runs, one process alone. The sliding window's gate reduced, when a loop's period is its own ticker's interval, to a comparison of this tick's lease-acquire delay against the previous tick's, so a lone process lost about a third of its ticks. Nobody would have found that by reading it: the tester drove ten real ticks of a real loop against real Postgres and counted, then found the same thing in the browser suite's single-process log, where a skipped tick had fired 18 ms earlier than the one before it. What the two-process rows could not see is that they never ran the loop alone. A property worth pinning at N processes is worth pinning at one, and the three rows now stand separately: once-per-period, mutual exclusion, and no-skip-when-alone.

Round 3's finding is a written-down wrong invariant rather than a line of code. recordPassOn's comment said 'a pass cut short by shutdown still ran and still served its period' - the behaviour, asserted as the intention - so a reader checking the code against the comment would have stopped there and found them agreeing. The merged behaviour was: the record is written after the pass returns, so a kill or a panic leaves the period unserved and the next tick runs it, and a graceful SIGTERM was the one exception, since the pass's context was cancelled but recordPassOn ran on a context of its own. The fix leaves the period unserved there too, and the comment now says what happens instead and that it said the opposite. The statement of that behaviour reached the architect in a message rather than in this file, because the handoff was already committed when the question was asked: the gap was found after the phase closed, not withheld during it.

Two consequences of that fix, named rather than left to be discovered. A cut-short tick now returns false, and internal/dispatch/delivery/intake.go is the one caller that reads that answer (to decide its bind throttle): harmless at shutdown, since the process is going, and said in a comment at that call site. And a pass that finished microseconds before the cancellation arrived is read as cut short and records nothing, costing one early pass in the next period; that is the safe direction of the two errors and is deliberately not tightened.

Round 3 also corrected two headSha fields in this file that named no commit: 'fe0c2f1c2a6317e1e6e4b0dbc7e0c3f0eca61b0e' (the real head is fe0c2f1c2a631bed1cab81d9548dd49b10c2cf51), which the tester found, and '18438f0b6367a1e2b5c9e8b2a0bbb0d2dd3dba77' (the real head is 18438f0b63673b3aa958c9d6c0c1c911986c00cd), which looking for the first one found. How they were produced: each proof row was written with the short id in hand from the push output and the rest of the hex typed to fill the field rather than read back from 'jj log -r <id> -T commit_id'. Nothing between writing them and the tester's check resolved them - not this file's own shape check, which refuses only an empty field, and not any reader - so forty-hex values pointing at nothing travelled as evidence. The mechanism is the finding, and the second one is its proof: one wrong id is a slip, two of the same shape is a habit. Every headSha here has now been resolved against the repository, which is the check that was missing.

A harness pitfall the next role should not spend an hour on: this pod's nats-server is long-lived, and its ENVOY_NOTIFICATIONS stream keeps a 72-hour duplicate window, so after many local runs TestTheOutboxPublishesEachEventOnceAcrossBothProcesses fails with 'the notification stream holds nothing this row published' - its publishes are suppressed as duplicates rather than stored. It is harness state and not the change: stop the role's nats-server, remove /legion/harness/natsdata and re-run setup.sh. setup.sh now says so at its end.

Three defects were found only by surfaces, not by reading the code. The browser suite went red across five specs because the relay kept a cursor and nothing else, and the suite truncates the database between scenarios, so the ids restart below the cursor and the live stream is silent for ever; the fix reuses the delivery hub's own reset rule (eventCursorCheck) and ends every open subscription. Running the document suite under concurrent writes found the two cursor races above. And the two-process rig built its processes' database URL without the password, so every row passed locally against a trust-authenticated server and failed 28P01 in CI.

The delivery standby has three bind outcomes rather than two, and the third was discovered in CI: on a fresh bus the reconciliation is leased, so exactly one process creates each durable and every other process's subscribe is answered 'consumer not found' until that create lands. That is a wait, not a fault. The same lease is shared by the two intakes of one process, so a throttle that recorded a pass the lease had refused could leave a durable uncreated for a settings poll.
